rows.text: Honestly, a sign-in screen is a sign-in screen — my team could handle this without training, which is more than I can say for the first week of Vault. The password reset flow with the code shown right on screen is simple enough, though showing the code on screen instead of emailing it would confuse my coordinators who expect an email. Nothing here would slow us down.

Honestly, this looks easier than half the systems I use daily — one card, two fields, and the password rules are shown as you type instead of after you fail. My team of nine would get through sign-up without a single call to me, which is more than I can say for our Vault onboarding. The only thing I'd trip on is the workspace name disappearing on another machine — I move between my office desktop and a laptop at client sites constantly.

For me personally it reads straightforward — a ten-step guided rail with lock reasons is far gentler than docuBridge ever was, and my junior associates could follow it without me hovering. My hesitation is the opposite problem: it may be too simplified for the parallel, non-linear way we actually work, where CMC content is being assembled while the admin forms are still pending. I don't file one drug like a bedtime story; I run six sequences at once.

Honestly, the step-by-step rail with locked steps and plain-language lock reasons would be easy for me, and frankly easier still for the two juniors on my team — it is far gentler than docuBridge. My worry is the opposite problem: it may be too simplified for someone running 15 sequences in parallel; I do not see how I jump between dossiers or work steps out of order when a client sends Module 3 late. The "no regulatory background needed" pitch is not a selling point to me — it is a red flag for who they think the user is.

Honestly, this looks simpler than half of what my team wrestles with in Vault RIM — one button, two fields, and you're into Module 1. The ID format validation with a plain-language error message is the kind of guardrail my junior associates need. My only hesitation is those native browser prompt/confirm dialogs for renaming and deleting; that feels flimsy and would make me pause mid-click.

Honestly, this looks simpler than half of what my team wrestles with in Vault RIM — one button, two fields, and you're into a Module 1 workspace. The format validation on the Dossier ID with a plain-English error message would save my juniors from typos. My only hesitation is the browser popup dialogs for renaming and deleting; those feel flimsy and my people will fat-finger them.

Honestly, this looks more approachable than docuBridge for the drafting side — the three-column layout with the section tree and the M1–M5 tabs mirrors how we already think in eCTD, so my team wouldn't be lost. My worry is the density: glyphs, chips, mode toggles, ghost buttons — my junior associates would manage, but I'd need a solid half-day training before I let anyone touch a client dossier. The rigid Dossier ID format with a placeholder escape hatch is sensible; we often don't have the ID at kickoff.

For me personally this looks manageable — the three-column layout with a section tree and status glyphs is not far from how docuBridge organizes an eCTD backbone, so my team would orient quickly. The module tabs M1–M5 and the "3/7 required sections complete" progress rail are exactly the kind of tracking I currently maintain by hand in Excel. My only hesitation is the density: chips for Help, Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence, Journey, Application Viewer and Audit all at once is a lot for a junior associate on day one.

Honestly, for me and my team the mechanics look manageable — a section tree, click a section, pick Upload or Author, that's not far from how we work in Vault. Where I stumble is the chat itself: my reviewers aren't prompt-writers, and "tell it about the submission" puts the burden on us to know what to feed it. The little glyphs and badges (✶AI, req/opt) I'd learn, but I'd want a legend somewhere.

For me personally, the chat layout is familiar enough — it reads like texting a junior writer, and the tree/panel/status-rail layout maps to what my team already knows from Vault. My worry is the mode toggles: "Author in-app" then "Draft with AI" versus "Sample & edit" is two layers of choices before you type a word, and I can see my newer associates picking the wrong path. The Enter-to-send with streaming replies is fine; nobody on my team would struggle with that part.

On paper this looks manageable — the layout mirrors what my team already knows from Vault and docuBridge, with a section tree, sequences, and a validation panel in familiar places. My worry is my associates who live in Excel trackers: terms like "working sequence" and "Make active" will need training, because activating the wrong sequence before an export is exactly the kind of mistake a junior makes at 6 p.m. on a filing day.

For me and my team, this looks manageable — the layout mirrors what we know from docuBridge, with sequences, a validation card with rule codes, and pass/fail badges, so my senior associates would find their feet quickly. My only hesitation is that the readiness signals are scattered across a summary card, a validation card, and a sequences card in a side rail; on a busy filing day I want one unambiguous "you may export" gate, not three places to cross-check.

The Portfolio page itself looks manageable — dossier rows with gate and fee chips at a glance is exactly how my team thinks. But I stopped cold at "reachable by URL; the top bar does not link to it" for both Registry and Correspondence. If my associates have to bookmark hidden URLs to reach the product registry, that is a training burden and an error waiting to happen — in Veeva everything is in the navigation.

The Portfolio page itself looks manageable — cards, chips, an "Open" link, my team could handle that. But two of the three pages are only reachable by typing a URL, which is a non-starter; half my associates would never find the Registry or Correspondence pages, and I'd be the one fielding the "where is it" emails. Re-typing dossier IDs like "e123456" into fields is exactly the kind of manual step that causes wrong-dossier errors.

Honestly, from what I read this looks easier than what my team wrestles with in docuBridge — a step rail, plain-language guidance, autosave. My worry is the opposite problem: it may be too simplified for people like us who file dozens of sequences and don't need every term explained. The 3D "submission tower" strikes me as a gimmick I'd turn off if I could.

For me personally it looks quite easy — a step rail, a resume feature, plain-language explanations. Frankly it may be easier than docuBridge, which took my juniors months to learn. My only hesitation is the 3D "submission tower"; I don't need my dossier in 3D, I need to know which documents are missing.

Honestly, it's a login screen — if I couldn't handle this after six years of fighting eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit, I'd have bigger problems. The disabled-until-filled button, Enter-to-submit, and live password feedback are the kind of small polish that means fewer stupid errors. The only friction I foresee is the workspace-name-stored-in-browser thing; I work across my desk PC and a validation room machine, so a blank workspace label on device two would throw me for a second.

Honestly, this is just a login and signup screen — I'd get through it in under a minute, same as any SaaS tool we use. The password rules with the live countdown are the kind of thing I'd barely notice. Nothing here is harder than logging into GlobalSubmit.

For me personally this would be easy — honestly easier than my current eCTD Office workflow, since the ten-step rail with locks mirrors how I already sequence a filing in my head. The inline Dossier ID format check on blur is a nice touch that would save me the dumb typos. My only friction worry is bouncing between the journey and a separate dossiers page for the Module builder — context switching mid-assembly is where mistakes happen.

For me personally this would be easy — honestly easier than my day job in eCTD Office, since the left rail and lock reasons basically replicate the checklist I keep in my head. My only friction point is the split between the journey and the separate Module builder page; I'd want to live in the module view, not get bounced out and back for a gate check.

For someone who lives in eCTD Office all day, this looks trivially easy — two fields and a create button is less friction than setting up a new application in most publishing tools. The placeholder-ID escape hatch is smart because in real life we start assembling Module 3 months before REP issues the Dossier ID. My only ease concern is the native browser prompt for setting the real ID later — typing an ID into a bare prompt() box with no validation preview feels clunky for something that "moves all documents, sequences and history."

For me this looks trivially easy — a tile grid, a create form with two fields, and you're straight into Module 1. Honestly it's simpler than eCTD Office's project setup, and the placeholder-ID escape hatch means I'm not blocked waiting on REP to come back with the real number.

For someone who lives in eCTD Office all day, this looks pretty approachable — the M1–M5 tabs, section tree with completion glyphs, and a right rail showing "3/7 required sections complete" map cleanly onto how I already think about a sequence. The Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A split per section is exactly the decision I make fifteen times a day. My only ease worry is the sample pre-fill: editing "every field" of a worked example is fine for one section, but across a whole Module 2 that's a lot of manual replacement where a missed sample value would be dangerous.

For someone who lives in eCTD Office all day, this looks straightforward — the three-column layout with a section tree, glyphs, and a right-rail readiness panel mirrors how I already think about a sequence. The Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A tabs match exactly the three things I actually do with a section. My only friction would be the sample pre-fill: I'd be paranoid about missing a "sample" tag on some field and shipping worked-example text into a real 1.2.5.

Honestly, this looks easy — easier than what I do today bouncing between Word templates, SharePoint, and eCTD Office. The tree-plus-panel layout mirrors how I already think about a sequence, and Upload / Author / Mark N/A covers the three things I actually do with a section. The chat drafting itself is trivial to operate; the hard part is knowing what to feed it, and the prompt hint helps there.

For me this would be easy — I live in eCTD Office all day, and a section tree with req/opt badges and gate flags maps directly onto how I already think about a sequence. The chat itself is basically typing sponsor details into a box, which is less friction than hunting for the last approved template on SharePoint. My only stumble would be the "Author" fallback button that's actually hidden under "Sample & edit" — I'd waste a minute looking below the chat like the message says.

Honestly, this looks pretty easy for someone like me — it mirrors the mental model I already have from eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit: sequences, leafs, validation findings with rule codes. The tile-to-workspace flow and the side-rail cards seem straightforward, and the "Show all 12 errors" toggle is fine. My only friction point is that validation being split between a pre-computed structural check and a separate "Run full check" button means I'd have to remember to click the second one every time before export.

For someone who lives in eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit daily, this layout reads as familiar — sequences, leaf counts, module tabs, rule codes. I'd figure it out in an afternoon. The only friction I see is the split between the pre-computed structural check and the "Run full check (PDF conformance)" button; I'd have to remember that a green badge might not mean the PDFs were actually checked yet.

For someone who lives in eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit all day, this looks manageable — the portfolio dashboard with gate and fee chips is basically what I keep in a SharePoint tracker now. But making Registry and Correspondence reachable only by typing a URL is bizarre; I'd forget the paths within a week and so would anyone I train. Typing dossier IDs by hand into the Correspondence page instead of picking from a list is asking for e123456-style typos.

Honestly, most of this maps to how I already work in eCTD Office and a tracker spreadsheet, so I'd pick it up in an afternoon. The dossier rows with gate and fee chips are exactly what I chase down manually today. But having to reach Registry and Correspondence by typing URLs is amateur hour — I shouldn't need bookmarks to find core pages in a submissions tool.

For me personally this would be easy — honestly easier than eCTD Office, since the step rail and M1-M5 tabs map to how I already think about a sequence. The dossier ID validation with the format hint is the kind of guardrail I wish our current tools had. My only friction point is the "no regulatory background needed" framing; I don't need the hand-holding narrative, so I'd want a way to skip straight to the module workspace without the story journey.

For me personally this would be easy — arguably too easy, since I already live in eCTD Office all day and know what a control number and REP transaction are. The three-column layout with a step rail and module tabs M1–M5 maps cleanly onto how I actually think about a sequence, so I'd find my way around in minutes. My only friction concern is the "story" framing adding clicks between me and the actual document slots.

Honestly this looks easier than half the systems I use — it's just a sign-in card like any other website, and I like that the button stays greyed out until I've filled things in so I can't submit half-done. The password rule with the live countdown would actually help me instead of guessing why my password got rejected. My only worry is the number of chips after login (Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence, Guided journey) — I'd probably hover over all of them nervously the first time not knowing which one I'm supposed to click for my filing.

Honestly, this looks easier than half the internal portals I use — it's just a sign-in card, and I like that the button stays disabled until I've filled things in so I can't submit half-done. The password rule with the live character countdown is the kind of hand-holding I actually appreciate. The only thing that would slow me down is figuring out whether I create the workspace or whether my manager already did.

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I do now — I basically live in Word templates and a checklist my manager made, so a left rail with 10 steps and locked steps that tell you why they're locked would be a relief. The "You're here" and "Done" markers are exactly the kind of hand-holding I need on my first filings. The only part that sounds hard is the stuff the tool can't do for me, like waiting weeks for a Company ID from the OSIP mailbox.

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I do now, which is digging through Word templates on our shared drive and emailing my manager to ask what comes next. The 10-step journey with locked steps and plain-language reasons is exactly how my brain wants this to work. The only part I'd stumble on is the Dossier ID and Company ID stuff, but the tool seems to hold your hand through even that, including the "continue while it's pending" option, which is realistic because that wait genuinely takes weeks.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — we track dossier numbers in an Excel sheet and a folder tree on the shared drive, so tiles with progress bars would be a relief. The form seems simple enough that I could create a dossier without asking anyone. My only worry is the ID format check; I'd probably get the red error the first time because I still mix up what HC actually issues.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — right now I keep track of our dossier info in a Word tracker on the shared drive, so tiles with progress bars would be a nice upgrade. The form only asks for two fields, and I like that the ID format error tells me exactly what's expected. The only part I'd fumble is the "draft ID — set real" thing popping up as a plain browser prompt; that feels easy to mistype with no way to double-check before it "moves all documents and history".

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I do now — our Word templates don't tell you anything, so I'm constantly pinging my manager asking "is 1.2.5 required for this product?" A section tree with required-vs-not-required glyphs and a "What Health Canada needs here" box would save me so many awkward questions. The three-column layout with tabs M1-M5 might feel busy at first, but it's the same eCTD structure I'm already trying to learn, so I think I'd get it within a day or two.

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I do now — I'm juggling Word templates on a shared drive and I never know which version is current. The three-column layout with the section tree and glyphs feels like something I could pick up in a day. The only bit that might trip me up is the Dossier ID format rule, but they even give a placeholder option, which is exactly what I'd need since we usually don't have the ID until later.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — I basically live in Word templates and email chains, so having a chat that asks me for the details it needs instead of leaving blanks sounds way less intimidating. I'd probably figure out the tree and the Upload/Author tabs quickly. The one thing that would trip me up is that the confirmation after saving is only announced to screen readers, so I might sit there wondering if it actually saved and what I'm supposed to do next.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — I spend hours copying from old Word templates on our shared drive, so a chat that asks me for the details it needs sounds manageable. The layout with the section tree and the "req"/"opt" badges is like a checklist, which I like. My only worry is all the little icons and modes — Upload vs Author in-app vs Mark N/A vs Sample & edit — I'd probably click around a bit before I found the right one.

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I do now — right now I keep a checklist in Excel and email PDFs back and forth, so having a card that just says "3/4 required sections complete" would save me so much second-guessing. The tiles and progress bars feel like something I could pick up in a day. The only part I'd probably need a senior to explain is the sequences card — I've only ever worked on sequence 0000, so "working: 0001" and "Make active" would confuse me at first.

Honestly, once I found the right cards it seems manageable — the checklist with Documents, Fee and Valid eCTD ticks is exactly how I track things in my Excel now. But the workspace has a lot going on: module tabs, a section tree, chips, plus two different cards on the right, and I'd probably need a senior to show me the sequence part. The "Run full check" vs the pre-computed check distinction would confuse me the first few times.

The Portfolio page itself sounds manageable — cards, chips, and an "Open" link are basically what I'd expect from any dashboard. But having to reach the Registry and Correspondence pages by typing a URL would honestly lose me; I'd forget the address and end up emailing a senior asking where the page went. Once I'm on a page the forms with placeholders like "e123456" seem doable for someone at my level.

The Portfolio page itself sounds manageable for me — cards, chips, an Open link, that's not harder than the trackers we keep in Excel. But having to reach the Registry and Correspondence pages by typing a URL would honestly stop me; I'd never guess those exist, and I'd probably email a senior asking where the "notices" screen is. Once someone showed me the URLs I think I could use it day to day.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — everything I've learned so far has been from Word templates and asking my seniors what things mean, so a step-by-step flow that explains each term as you go sounds like it was made for someone like me. The three-column layout with the step rail seems intuitive enough. My only worry is the 3D tower thing might be more distracting than helpful when I just need to know what's missing.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — I live in Word templates on a shared drive and constantly ask my seniors what goes where, so a step rail that walks me through the journey and explains every term sounds like a relief. The "34% ready" chip and resuming where I left off would genuinely help me since I lose track of what's done across files. My only worry is the "Start over" button sitting right in the top bar — I'd be terrified of clicking it by accident.

Honestly, a sign-in card with two fields is about as simple as it gets, and I appreciate that the button stays disabled until things are filled in. The password rule with the live checkmark is helpful — I won't have to call IT to ask why my password was rejected. My only hesitation is that after sign-in I'm dropped onto a page full of chips like "Portfolio" and "Registry" with no explanation of where to start.

Honestly, a sign-in card with two fields is about the level of technology I'm comfortable with, so I don't foresee trouble getting in. The password reset with a code and a "Back to sign in" button seems manageable even for someone like me who still keeps SOPs in binders. My only hesitation is that these screens always look easy until something goes wrong and IT has to get involved.

For someone like me who mostly lives in Acrobat and paper SOPs, the step-by-step rail with plain-language lock reasons looks manageable — I could probably follow it without calling IT. My worry is the pieces that shove me elsewhere, like the separate Module builder page and the 3D tower thing, which sounds like decoration I'd have to learn to ignore. If it truly holds my hand one step at a time, I could use it.

Honestly, the step-by-step left rail with locks and "You're here" is the kind of hand-holding I'd want — it reads more like a checklist than software, and I live in checklists. The 3D "tower" of module tiles I could do without; I just need a plain list of what's in and what's missing. My worry is the Module builder living on a separate dossiers page — jumping between screens is where people like me lose track.

Honestly, the basic flow — click a button, enter two fields, open the dossier — sounds simple enough even for someone like me who still lives in Acrobat and paper SOPs. The inline validation message telling me the exact ID format is the kind of hand-holding I appreciate. What would trip me up is the jargon-dense workspace it drops me into afterward — section trees, submission towers, readiness flags — that's a lot to absorb without a training session and an SOP behind it.

Honestly, this part looks manageable even for someone like me — one button, two fields, and a clear error message if you get the ID format wrong. I sign off on submissions rather than assemble them, but I could follow this screen without a training session. My only hesitation is the number of navigation chips up top; I'd want an SOP telling me which ones I actually need.

Honestly, there's a lot on the screen — three columns, module tabs, chips, glyphs — and I'd need someone to walk me through it once or twice before I'd be comfortable. That said, the section tree with circles and checkmarks maps to how I already track completeness on paper, so I could learn it. The "Dossier ID must be one letter + 6-7 digits" hint is the kind of plain instruction I appreciate.

For someone like me who lives in Acrobat and paper SOPs, this looks busier than what I'm used to — three columns, module tabs, glyphs, chips everywhere. That said, the section tree with the circle/half-circle/checkmark markers mirrors how I mentally track a submission, so once oriented I think I could follow it. My worry is the little symbols and toggles ("⊘ Mark N/A", mode switches) that assume you already know the conventions.

The screen layout itself sounds manageable — a section tree, a work panel, badges for required versus optional — that maps onto how I already think about a dossier. But the AI chat part assumes I know what to tell it and in what form, and I don't type free-form prompts into software for a living. I'd also worry I'd click "Use this draft" without realizing the review step lives somewhere else entirely under a different tab.

I could probably manage the chat part itself — typing sponsor details into a box isn't hard, even for someone like me who mostly lives in Acrobat and paper SOPs. What worries me is everything around it: three panels, glyphs, badges, mode toggles between "Draft with AI" and "Sample & edit" — that's a lot of interface to learn before I'd trust myself not to click the wrong thing. And the fact that the save confirmation is only announced to a screen reader means I'd sit there wondering whether anything actually happened.

Honestly, this looks busier than what I'm used to — module tabs, section trees, side rails with cards, chips everywhere. I sign off on packages others assemble, so I mostly work in Acrobat and our validated vault, and I'd need someone to walk me through where the validation results live versus where the export button is. That said, the traffic-light readiness flags (Documents, Fee, Valid eCTD) are the kind of at-a-glance summary I could actually use for sign-off.

Honestly, this looks busier than what I'm used to — module tabs, section trees, chips everywhere — but the actual validate-and-export path seems manageable: check the readiness flags, run the validation, hit Export. I'd need someone to walk me through sequences and "make active" the first couple of times. Compared to me flipping through a 200-page validation report in Acrobat, the card with the pass/fail badge is actually simpler.

The Portfolio page itself sounds manageable — cards, rows, an export button — that I could handle. But I'm being told the Registry and Correspondence pages are only reachable by typing a URL? At my age and with my patience, if it's not on a menu, it doesn't exist. I'd be phoning IT or the RA associate to find these pages every time.

The Portfolio page itself I could probably manage — cards, rows, an export button, that's not far off the dashboards I already tolerate. But I'm told two of the three pages, Registry and Correspondence, are only reachable by typing a URL, and I don't keep URLs in my head; if it's not a button on the screen, half my staff will never find it. The Correspondence page with three stacked panels and buttons like "Record s.6 action" would take me a training session and a written SOP before I'd touch it.

The step-by-step rail and the plain-language explanations would honestly help me — I'm not a regulatory affairs specialist by training, I review what others assemble, and most eCTD tools assume you already know everything. The dossier ID validation with the CESG helper text is the kind of hand-holding I'd appreciate. The 3D "submission tower" I could do without; I don't need my modules floating in space, I need to know what's missing.

Honestly, this looks approachable even for someone like me who still prints out the guidance documents. The step-by-step rail and plain-language explanations would help, though I worry the "3D submission tower" is decoration I'd have to click around rather than a table I can print and review. The draft dossier ID option is sensible since Health Canada's REP process can take a while.

Honestly, this is just a login screen, so yes, I could use it — I set up my own LORENZ and CESG accounts without help. The live password helper text and the Enter-to-submit are the kind of small things that keep me from fumbling. My one hesitation is "one workspace per client company": with 6-8 sponsor clients, does that mean I'm creating and juggling eight separate logins or workspaces? That could get tedious fast.

Honestly, this is just a sign-in card, and it looks about as simple as these things get — email, password, one button, Enter key works. The password reset with the on-screen code is easy enough, though I'd note that in twelve years I've never had a reset flow show me my own code on the page. For someone like me juggling six clients, creating a workspace per client seems straightforward, though that's six sets of credentials to manage.

For me personally this would be easy — almost too easy, since I already know what a dossier ID and Company ID are, and the wizard hand-holds through steps I do from memory. The gated left rail with plain-language lock reasons is a sensible structure, and the disabled Continue button until required documents are placed mirrors how I actually run my own checklists.

For me personally this would be easy — almost too easy, since it's clearly built for people who've never touched an eCTD. The linear 10-step rail with lock reasons and the on-blur Dossier ID format check would save my junior clients a lot of back-and-forth. My worry is the reverse: as an experienced preparer I'd want to jump around non-linearly, and a padlocked journey could slow me down.

For someone like me who lives in Word and eValidator, this looks manageable — a tile grid, one button to create a dossier, and clear inline fields is nothing intimidating. My only hesitation is that renaming and deleting go through raw browser prompt boxes, which feel flimsy and easy to mis-click when I'm juggling six clients' files.

For me this looks manageable — a tile list, one button, two fields is not asking much of someone who lives in Word and eValidator. The ID format validation with an inline example is the kind of guardrail I'd want, since I've seen sponsors mangle the e-number more times than I can count. My only friction would be the browser prompt/confirm dialogs for renaming and deleting; those feel flimsy and easy to mis-click for something as consequential as deleting an entire dossier.

For someone like me who has lived in these modules for twelve years, the three-column layout with a section tree and status glyphs would feel familiar — it maps to how I already think about an ANDS. My worry is for the volume of clicking between tabs and chips; I keep everything in Word and my own checklists, and learning a whole workspace has a cost. But the "Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A" choice per section is exactly the decision I make anyway, so the mental model fits.

For me this looks manageable — the three-column layout with a section tree and status glyphs mirrors how I already track sections in my own checklists, so I'd find my way around. The one thing I'd stumble on is the sample pre-fill: editing every pre-populated field is fine for me, but it's an extra pass of work compared to starting blank, and I'd want a way to clear all samples at once rather than hunt for little "sample" tags.

Mechanically it looks easy enough — click the section, type a prompt, hit Send, accept the draft; I could do that between client calls. What would slow me down is the hunting: the review step lives under a different mode ("Sample & edit"), and the fallback "Author" button isn't where the error message says it is. I don't have time to guess where things are hiding.

The layout itself — tree, panel, gate flags — mirrors how I already think about a dossier, so I could navigate it fine. But chatting a document into existence is a new habit for someone who drafts in Word against her own checklists, and I'd be slower here, not faster, at least at first. The Enter-to-send and streaming bubbles are fine; my worry is the effort shifts from writing to verifying.

For someone who spent years staring at eValidator output, this layout would come naturally — sequences, leaf counts, rule codes, all in the places I'd expect. The M1–M5 tabs and section tree mirror how I already think about a dossier, so I doubt I'd need training. My only friction point is the two-tier validation: I'd have to remember the on-screen status is only the structural pre-check until I press "Run full check".

For me this would be manageable — the layout mirrors how I already think: sequences, leaf counts, a validation card with rule codes. My one friction point is the split between the pre-computed structural check and the separate "Run full check (PDF conformance)" button; I'd worry a client clicks Export trusting the quick check without ever running the deep one.

The Portfolio page itself looks manageable — cards, gate chips, fee status, that's the kind of dashboard I'd actually use across my six sponsors. But two of the three pages are only reachable by typing a URL? I'm not going to remember /correspondence, and neither will my clients when I hand this over. That alone would generate support calls to me.

Mechanically it looks easy — the step rail, the dossier tiles, the resume-where-you-left-off all sound simpler than juggling my Word checklists. My worry is the opposite problem: it may be too easy, letting a sponsor click through to "Ready to file" without understanding what they've attested to. The dossier ID validation with a placeholder option is a sensible touch I'd actually use.

This is a login screen — if my team can't get through this, we have bigger problems. The live password helper and Enter-to-submit are the kind of polish I'd expect from any modern SaaS. Nothing here would slow me down.
